theme: “I AM the vine”; the Paraclete; sorrow turned to joy
readingInstruction: Read John 15:1-16:33. Jesus continues his teaching in the Upper Room: the vine and the branches, the world’s hatred, and the work of the Holy Spirit. It ends with sorrow turned to joy and a word of victory. Read 15:1-17 slowly.
settingTheScene: The disciples have heard that Jesus is going away, and they are troubled. Jesus has told them to love one another and has promised the Spirit. Now, as they leave the upper room (14:31), he continues to teach, perhaps on the way to the garden. The image of the vine was familiar: Israel was often called God’s vine in the Old Testament, and was often unfruitful. Jesus says that he is the true vine.
observation: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser” (15:1).
“I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (15:5).
“Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (15:13).
“You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit” (15:16).
“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you” (15:18).
“It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you” (16:7).
“When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth” (16:13).
“In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (16:33).
interpretation:
“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” This is the seventh and last of John’s “I AM” statements with a picture. Israel had been the vine that failed to bear good fruit (Isaiah 5), and Jesus is the true Israel who does. The Father is the gardener. He removes the branches that bear no fruit and prunes those that do, so that they bear more. Pruning is painful, but its purpose is fruitfulness.

The key word is “abide.” It means to remain, to stay connected. “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.” A branch has no life of its own. It lives by being joined to the vine. Apart from Jesus we can do nothing. Abiding in him means trusting him, keeping his words in us, praying, and loving as he loves. The fruit is Christlike character, and also lasting work and joy: “that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full.”

The vine teaches about union with Christ, which is at the center of the New Testament. We are not merely following his example; we are joined to him. His life flows into ours. The result is love: “As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love.” The command is to love one another, and the model is his own sacrifice: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” He calls them friends, not servants, because he has made known to them all that he has heard from the Father. And in verse 16: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” The initiative is his.

Then he warns that the world will hate them, as it hated him. Persecution will come. But the Spirit will come as Helper, testify about Jesus, convict the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment, and guide them into all the truth. The disciples are sad that Jesus is leaving, but he says it is to their advantage, because the Spirit will come. He uses the picture of a woman in labor: her pain turns to joy when the child is born. The disciples will weep, but their sorrow will become joy, and no one will take it from them.

The discourse ends with a promise: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.” It is the victory he will win on the cross.
connection: Isaiah 5:1-7, Psalm 80:8-16, and Hosea 10:1 describe Israel as a vine. Jeremiah 2:21 says Israel became a degenerate wild vine. Ezekiel 15 and 19:10-14 speak of the vine’s fruitlessness. Galatians 5:22-23 lists the fruit of the Spirit. Romans 6:5 and 11:17-24 speak of being united with Christ and grafted in. Colossians 1:27 speaks of Christ in you, the hope of glory. 1 John 2:6, 3:24, and 4:13 speak of abiding. Philippians 1:6 says God will complete his good work.
application:
Ask how you are abiding: in prayer, in the Word, in fellowship? Choose one practice to strengthen.

Think about a season of pruning in your life. Ask the vinedresser what fruit he is growing.

Say “I have overcome the world” to yourself the next time you are afraid.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you abide in the true vine.
Confess where you try to produce fruit apart from him.
Thank him for turning sorrow into joy.
